The main problem with this course was the labs. The labs were not organized well, and most of them were too long to realistically complete within the 4-hour lab period, especially considering that around 30 minutes of the time was also used for quizzes. In many cases, the labs felt as if they had been prepared at the last minute.
The third lab in particular required far too much work for the amount of time given. Additionally, our section had the first lab hour of the week for 4 out of the 5 labs. Because of this, we were often at a disadvantage compared to the later sections.
For example, we were not informed beforehand that we could obtain the OPAMP component before the lab session, while the later sections were informed about this. Since we were the first section, we were also the first ones to take the quizzes. The quizzes across sections were very similar, usually with only minor differences. This meant that students in later sections could prepare using information from our quiz, while we had no such advantage. However, in the one lab where our section completed the lab after the other sections, the quiz was not shared with us.
For a course that serves as a foundation for many future courses, the labs became the most stressful part rather than a productive learning experience.

We encountered many problems with both the lab TAs and the grader TAs throughout the semester. In the second lab, our preliminary work was graded before the actual deadline. Additionally, some grades were reduced from 100 to 80 due to something that was not even included in the lab requirements. After we contacted the grader TA, the grades were changed back. However, this situation showed that there were consistent grading criteria for the lab, and that grading depended heavily on the individual grader.
Regarding the lab TAs, there was also serious inconsistency in the way students were treated. In particular, I observed that one of the lab TAs, Ramal Hasanli, appeared to treat certain students more favorably, showing them more patience and support compared to others. This created an unfair lab environment.
In the third lab, one of the TAs informed us that there was no realistic way to complete the lab checks on time and mentioned that this had also been a problem in previous years. When we informed the head TAs, Fuat Arslan and Ramal Hasanli, we were told that we could receive an extension because our section had not been informed beforehand that some components could be obtained before the lab session. However, despite the extension, 10 points were still deducted from each delayed check.
Some TAs evaluated checks according to clear criteria, while others barely examined the work. This made the grading process feel unfair and inconsistent. Near the end of the lab, some TAs discussed canceling certain checks while others continued grading normally, again depending entirely on the TA. Some checks were cancelled only at the last 5 minutes due to errors, which were simply due to the components. 
Later, an email was sent by Ramal Hasanli stating that no further objections would be accepted and asking students to stop complaining to avoid excessive noise, even though many students were simply trying to raise concerns about fairness.
